column3: A pyxis with a lid. A round container covered with a lid. The lid is decorated with a raised ridge, in the centre there is a depression in which the round handle is set. This may have been used to hold cosmetics. Greek, Cycladic.
A figure of a ram in alabaster. There is a perforation through the side near the spine.
An altar cruet in silver, with a lid, beaked lip and a S-curved handle. There is an inscription around the waist which reads: Pray for ye soul of thor Knowles. Possibly Irish.
An amber flask with two handles. The front is decorated with two raised circular shapes, the smaller one on top of the larger one.

Bes is an ancient Egyptian deity, identified by ostrich feather headdress. Bes was a protector of households, but in particular women, mothers and childbirth and the warding off of evil spirits. Representations of Bes were often worn as amulets to protect the wearer.

A 15th century AD Gothic panel portion showing an angel holding a scroll in the left hand and leaning on an openwork panel with floral decoration. This may be a portion of the rood screen from Exeter Cathedral which was taken down in the 1840s.

column2: Apollo as the Genius of the Arts
column3: Apollo, the Classical god of light, poetry, music, healing and prophecy, was often used to represent the trades, arts and professions. Here he is their protector. There is a bird of prey on his shoulder and a lamb by his left foot. He wears a laurel wreath on his head and carries a pomegranate. The figure is naked except for narrow red bands to which are attached the symbols of trades, professions, crafts and artistic pursuits of the many guilds of the time. Decoration is confined to the front of the statue suggesting that the piece was made to stand in a corner. The feet are not original. Augsburg, Germany.
Lebes gamikos are a distinctive Greek wedding vessel, believed to have gifted to a bride. This vase a slim body and two upright handels. There are different scenes on each side; a woman is seated.
column7: 4th century BC, Classical Greek, Late Classical Greece

column3: A Lebes gamikos is a Greek wedding gift. Its role was to carry the water which was sprinkled over the bride in the ceremony. Red figure painting was an invention of the Athenians in the sixth-century BC. South Italian Greek colonies, including Apulia, continued red-figure vase production after its decline in Athens. There are painted scenes on either side of the object. On one, a woman seated on a rock cradles a dish and on the other, a winged Eros, god of love, clutches a mirror in his right hand. Both figures have rounded bodies, necklaces, bracelets and anklets. Eros wears a beaded bandolier.

This charm or amulet, originally owned by the Butler family of Garnavilla, near Cahir, Co. Tipperary, was traditionally invoked to protect cattle from disease. Family and neighbours dipped it in drinking water or hung it from the neck of a cow. The crystal ball, which weighs 200g, is mounted in a gilded copper or bronze frame with trefoil decoration and a hanging loop.
A barbed and tanged flint arrow-head. The barbs are much shorter than the tang and there is slight flaking on the surface.

A vase or lekythos, which would have contained oil. It has an a round base, basically cylindrical body though tapering towards the foot, a tall narrow neck which broadens out into a thick rim and a strap handle. The body is decorated with brown figures on a white background.
An axe-handle in antler, it splays out at the top being more curved at one side and straighter at the other.
An iron axehead with a widely splayed cutting edge.

A silver brooch in a thistle pattern. This is an example of a ball-type penannular brooch, which would have functioned as a dress or cloak fastener. The brooch has a silver penannular ring and has two solid globular terminals with criss-cross brambled decoration (hence the term thistle brooch) and terminals with the decorated ring ends extending beyond them. The pin is fitted into a thistle head with an expanded vertical terminal. The upper shank of the pin is rounded but the lower section is square, ending in a point. It has been suggested that this brooch is a nineteenth-century reproduction. However, the details of its manufacture and the slightly misshapen state of the pin do not support such speculation.

column2: BALLYBEG WESTBALLYBEG WEST Ballbeg Door Base
column3: In flat pasture, c. 200m S of Awbeg River. Complex of ruined 13th-century monastic buildings comprising church with cloister on S side (W end of church in line with mid-point of cloister) and claustral ranges to S, W and E (see plan Shine 1993, 108). Complex renovated in late-medieval period, when 4-storey rectangular tower built against N end of W claustral range and tower inserted into W end of church. Late-medieval rectangular tower (CO017-059002-), c. 70m to N, and columbarium (CO017-059003-), c. 25m to SE, also part of monastic complex.

In a flat pasture, c. 200m S of Awbeg River. Complex of ruined 13th-century monastic buildings comprising church with cloister on S side (W end of church in line with mid-point of cloister) and claustral ranges to S, W and E (see plan Shine 1993, 108). Complex renovated in late-medieval period, when 4-storey rectangular tower built against N end of W claustral range and tower inserted into W end of church. Late-medieval rectangular tower (CO017-059002-), c. 70m to N, and columbarium (CO017-059003-), c. 25m to SE, also part of monastic complex. CO017-059001

Found at Toome, Co. Antrim, the body and rim comprise eight pieces of beaten bronze, hammered to 1mm and riveted together. Horizontal rows of conical-headed rivets are functional and decorative. Four handles are of cast circular rings of ribbed cross-section. The rim was strengthened by eight vertical slender bronze stays riveted to the body. Cauldrons date to Late Bronze Age Europe, c. 800 BC. They were highly prized, often deposited in watery places.

A glazed earthenware jug with a round foot and strap handle. The body is decorated with brown and yellow vertical flutes. There is a brown dotted band around the neck and vertically at intervals on the body. This is a London-type baluster jug with Rouen-style decoration.
A bronze bell which is decorated with a cross on one face and circular bosses around the rim.

A bronze bell from the ninth century with the handle being part of the body of the bell. The bell is four-sided, splayed at the mouth and tapering towards the crown. The clapper is missing. The bell was found in Co. Westmeath.

This candelabrum was produced in the Belleek, Co. Fermanagh.The piece consists of the head of a stag supported by three scrolled acanthus leaves. The antlers form three branches and these support three candle holders in the form of sea urchins. The piece rests on a three-cornered flat base

This lead and ivory head of a leopard is an Edo ceremonial costume attachment from the royal court of of Benin, now incorporated into the modern republic of Nigeria. Much Benin art was looted following the violent Benin Expedition of 1897. The expedition was mounted to avenge the defeat by the Binis of a British invasion force that had violated Benin territory earlier in 1896. The number of Edo killed are unknown but acknowledged as very numerous. The story of Benin artwork is at the heart of an ongoing debate about cultural restitution.

This crozier head is carved in relief with inhabited foliated scrolls, mainly animals and birds, on the upright. The volute has three dimensional scenes, carved within it, on either side. One side shows two standing figures and one seated figure with the central figure touching the mouth of the seated figure. This is thought to refer to St John of Beverley (d. 721), Bishop of Hexham, curing a dumb boy. The reverse scene may relate to the Harrowing of Hell. The outer edge of the volute bears two incised inscriptions but they are indecipherable.

column2: Blue and white porcelain Chinese bowl
column3: A 17th or 18th century blue and white Chinese bowl with a slightly fluted rim. The outside of the bowl is decorated with panels showing river and mountain landscapes and panels with floral designs. The inside rim is decorated with a border of hatched lines.

Truncated biconical bead with a vertical perforation. Made of semi opaque, wound, blue glass with an opaque creamy white horizontal trail, around its centre. The bead has 7 ‘eyes’, four above and 3 below the centre line. These are irregularly placed and comprise an irregular circle of opaque white with 2 inner concentric circles of yellow and white with a blue glass central dot. Beads decorated with ‘eyes’ of layered glass are known from Egypt, Mesopotamia and Europe.
A bone comb with a single edge. It is decorated on both faces with criss-cross lines, parallel lines and circles.
A figure of a ram in bone. The ram is seated and there is a perforation through the body.
A carved bone plaque, depicting a deer amid foliage and a bird on a tree. There is a wide uncarved border surrounding the scene.
A plaque carved in relief on bone. It shows the figure of a naked man. He is twisted to the right, leaning on a rectangular object and holding a piece of cloth over his head. Coptic.
A bone point with a flat base. The base has three perforations from which the pin radiates out. The pin is rounded and tapers to a point.
A bone point with a roughly rounded butt tapering to a point
The bowl section of a maiolica jug in blue and gold lustre. It is decorated with vertical strips and floral decoration. The handle, spout and foot are missing. Italian, Deruta.
A brass bucket with a handle. It has a beaked front and a flat back and the body has a series of angled horizontal protrusions. This was used to hold holy water.

A cast socketed, faceted and looped axehead. Sub-rectangular cross section and the mouth slightly irregular and flared open. A flared convex cutting edge is bevelled and polished. Three parallel longitudinal ribs run from the edge of the mouth to just over half way towards the blade edge. These are even and on both faces. A thick loop sits on one side just above the socket mouth. The patina is mottled brown.

The vase has an angular profile and is decorated entirely with incised grooving. While a herring-bone motif rings the internal rim, the external decoration is zoned. There is a vertical ladder pattern on the rim/ neck, a band of alternate vertical and horizontal panels on the shoulder with a herring-bone design beneath, and the lower body has infilled chevron patterning with a herring-bone motif on the lower section. There is a circular hole in the base. This vessel was found in Mitchelstown, Co. Cork.

column2: Bronze Age riveted sheet bronze bucket
column3: A bucket of riveted sheet-bronze with a concave base and wheel-shaped base plate. The upper half is two sheets of bronze joined by flat-headed rivets and a rolled rim neck. The handles are lozenge-sectioned circular rings within ribbed staples riveted to the neck. Repoussé decoration forms horizontal bands of low bosses on the shoulder with filled pendant triangles below. This sort of decoration is known on continental buckets of the last millennium BC but is rarely found on Irish-British metalwork. Found in Cape Castle Bog, Armoy in Co. Antrim.

A yetholm spearhead with elongated leaf-shape blade with two crescentic perforations (lunate openings) abutting the midrib in the wings. A conical socket runs the length of the blade and contains two opposing circular peg-holes. Both blade edges have areas missing creating jagged edges which are not sharp. Spearheads with lunate openings are found in hoards across Britain and Ireland dating to the Late Bronze Age. These include the Dowris Hoard which gives its name to the last phase of the Irish Bronze Age - the Dowris Phase (900-600BC).

A yetholm spearhead with elongated leaf-shape blade with two crescentic perforations (lunate openings) abutting the midrib in the wings. A conical socket runs the length of the blade and contains two opposing circular peg-holes. Both blade edges have areas missing creating jagged edges which are not sharp. Spearheads with lunate openings are found in hoards across Britain and Ireland dating to the Late Bronze Age. These include the Dowris Hoard which gives its name to the last phase of the Irish Bronze Age - the Dowris Phase (900-600BC).
A ninth century bronze bell in good condition with the clapper missing. It has slight damage to one side. The bell was found at Bray, Co. Wicklow.

A ninth century bronze bell which is four-sided and rounded at the edges. It is splayed at the mouth and tapers towards the crown. The handle is not original and the clapper is missing. The bell was found in Co. Meath.

This is a small bronze hollow-cast quadrilateral bell. The bell has a crown with a circular inner opening and irregular angular outer edge. The shoulder gently curves into four sides. The lip opening is squared with a larger fragment missing on one side. On the opposing side in the same location is a small circular hole. Small quadrilateral bells were made throughout the Roman world using the cire-perdue process. They had a variety of functions including hanging on windchimes to bring good luck to families

A bronze bell which is circular and decorated in three zones with a pattern of acanthus leaves similar to that in stained glass and MSS of the period. The handle is a later addition and the clapper is missing.

A corpus in bronze with the feet apart and resting on a rectangular suppedaneum. The loin-cloth is long, knotted on the right and arranged in broad folds with a V-shaped fold in the front. The head is inclined down and to the right with the eyes closed.

column2: Bronze domed shield boss or phalera
column3: A phalera or shield boss of thin sheet bronze. A central domed disc is surrounded by a flat rim with a moulded edge. Along the rim are 25 moulded smaller circles, each with a central moulded dot. The central dome is concave with a tiny punched hole in the centre through which a small pointed rod of bronze was pushed to form a tiny loop and two pins on the reverse.

column2: Bronze Fibula or Brooch with coiled spring
column3: A bronze fibula with a broad coiled spring attached to a flattened loop. The bow is slightly arched and decorated with bands. It curves in underneath to form the clasp.

column2: Bronze fibula or Brooch with hinge
column3: A bronze fibula with a broad hinge with rounded terminals. The bow is partially arched and ends with a straight rod. It is decorated all over except for the curve. Germanic.
A figure of a griffin in bronze. The griffin is crouched with the forepart only represented. The figure has a flat underside.
Description: A figure of an animal in bronze. It is standing with a long tail and is horned.

column2: Bronze mount in shape of a dog
column3: A bronze mount in the form of an animal head, perhaps a dog, with three bar projections extending from the head. Possibly Roman.

column2: Bronze Statue of the god Horus
column3: This statuette, a standing hawk, is a typical form of the Egyptian God Horus. Hollow eye sockets were for a precious stone or metal inlay. The surface would have been highly polished and possibly overlaid with precious metal. From the seventh-century BC a vast number of bronze figurines of deities were produced in Egypt. Realistic statutory was common in the Late Period and fine metalwork used gold, silver and bronze. Subterranean galleries packed with mummified falcons were found at sites including Saqqara.

A cast unlooped, palstave axe with a stop or ledge-ridge joining the flanges across the top. The cutting edge is splayed, flanges large leaf shapes and the stop-ridge is straight. The flanges continue only slightly beyond the ridge. A Middle Bronze Age development of the flanged axe to create a more effective hafting technique. They occur throughout Europe with early examples in Ireland dating to the Killymaddy/Acton Park phase of the Middle Bronze Age (c. 1,600 BC). More.
A bronze two-handled vase with a tall neck and a flattened out-turned rim. There are rope handles on either side ending in a mask. The mask has an open mouth. Possibly Roman.

A bronze brooch of the spectacle type. It consists of thin strips of bronze coiled into two circular shapes with the strips twisted into a figure-of-eight between the circles. It has a bronze pin and two bronze loops at the back. Early Hallstatt style.

A bust of a child in faience (tin-glazed earthenware), the head is turned to one side and the child has chubby cheeks and short curly hair. The shoulder is damaged on the left. North Italian or German.

A bust of a woman in elephant ivory dated c. 18th Century. She is wearing a turban style head-dress secured by a brooch and a necklace with a pendant. Her mouth is open and some of her teeth are visible. The bust stands on a base of classical style. Dresden or Danzig attributed to Johann Christoph Ludwig von Lucke.

column2: Caltagrione Maiolica Jar in an owl shape
column3: A maiolica jar in the shape of an owl. The stopper in would have been in the shape of the owl head but is mising. It is decorated in a design known as peacock feather or peacock eye in blue, yellow and black. The back is undecorated. It may have contained oil or water with the head serving as the cup. Sicilian, probably Caltagirone.

column2: Caltagirone Drug-jar in maiolica, of a woman
column3: An Italian albarello or drug-jar of waisted cylindrical shape. On the centre-front is a portrait of a woman wearing a necklace in an oval frame which is surrounded by foliated, scroll work and sgraffito in blue, yellow and white. Similar to CG 36 B. These popular portrait pieces emphasize character rather than beauty. Sicilian, possibly Caltagirone.
A candelabrum in bronze, in the form of a male figure holding a candlestick in each hand. The figure is wearing a short tunic, a crown and he is bearded.
A bronze candlestick-holder. The holder is split.
A wooden, pricket-type candlestick.

A sheet-bronze bucket with a concave base protected by a base plate. The upper portion is two sheets riveted together with flat-headed rivets and a vertical neck with rolled rim. A riveted internal patch covers a large hole. Handles are lozenge-sectioned circular rings within ribbed staples. Repoussé decoration on the shoulder forms a band of rows of bosses with filled pendant triangles below. This is known on continental buckets of the last millennium BC but is rare on Irish-British metalwork. Found in Cape Castle Bog, Armoy in Co. Antrim
A plaque or mount carved in bone of an elephant head shown wearing some kind of harness.

column2: Carved Limestone Figure of a Monkey
column3: Carved from a single block this monkey Sits on a rectangular plinth, with knees drawn up. The upper arms reach out horizontally and the elbows rest on the knees. The forearms reach up and the fingers are wrapped around an elongated snout. The mouth is incised horizontally and the eyes are almond shape with rounded eyeballs. The air is long, falling vertically to the nape of the neck with a straight centre parting. The body and limbs are slender and long. A tail wraps around one thigh and curves under the hip.

Stone sphere carved with 4 large equidistant bosses surrounded by circles of nine smaller bosses. Three of the larger, have irregular incised line engraving. The bosses are relatively low profile with gentle, less defined definition between. Over 400 examples of this type of object are found in Scotland, Britain and Ireland have produced examples in dateable contexts from the Late Neolithic to the Iron Age.

A wooden female carved from a single piece of wood, she stands upright looking ahead with her arms by her sides. She is reported to have been found in a boat. Her hair is short and curled maybe indicating her youth. Female hair was decorated with ribbons, flowers, rings and amulets. Women of early Ancient and the Middle Kingdom preferred short hair. Wigs, used by the elite were coloured, blue, red or green decorated with precious stones and jewellery. Small figurines were models for larger sculptures, but were also Ka statues, carved in wood or stone and painted in likeness of their owner. They were receptacles for the ‘life-force’ or spirit of a body and stood in small niches in funerary houses or mortuary chapels. Boats were significant, believed to be the travel method of Gods.
A head of an animal carved in bone. Coptic.

This is a carving in ivory of a winged putto. He is sitting on the ground with his arms and legs around a goose. He holds a wing of the goose in his left hand and is smiling with his head turned to the right. Possibly German, 17th Century.

A carving of a human head in bone. The head is surrounded by an oval and there are three tubular openings running through the centre of the piece. It is probably Coptic - a style of artistic production by Christian Egyptians until the 12th century.

The Cashel Bell, which is a four-sided bell, is widest at the mouth and tapering towards the crown. The handle emerges from the crown in a semi-circular loop. The two gently curving faces are decorated with engraved crosses and all four faces are decorated with panels of a key pattern. The bell dates from the 9th century but the present handle is a 20th century replacement. This bell was found near Cashel in 1849.

A crackle-glaze celadon pot, perhaps a brush pot, with a removable, silver lid and a silver mount around the rim. The design on the lid is in repoussé with flowers and leaves between three cup-like designs with scrolled handles. The lid is marked with a leopards head crowned, lion passant, a date letter N within a rectangular shield and a makers mark (a three-leaved clover). The mark shows that the mounts were made in London in 1550. Chinese pot.

A dish or casserole with a cover and a handle on the left side. It is decorated with stylized deer, birds and rabbits between foliage. The cover also has a handle. This was probably used for cooking game. North American.
A figure of a boar with a prominent raised ridge running down the spine from the top of the forehead.
A ceramic figure of a rabbit with the ears lying back along his back.
A cermic head of a zebra.
A ceramic figure which is now badly abraded

This ceramic fragment of a human head, possibly from a figurine, was likely part of an effigy used for ceremonial purposes. Similar fragments have been attributed to the Teotihuacán style of Central México during the Classical Period. This fragment may have previously had common features (such as a lavish headdress) typical of other figures of the period.

This ceramic head, possibly a fragment off a larger figurine, likely originates from Mesoamerica. It may have been part of an effigy or standing figure, and similar examples have been dated back to the Aztec culture of Mesoamerican México.

column2: Mesoamerican Figurine - Fragment of a Face
column3: A head possibly from a figurine. It is ceramic, red/brown in colour with one eye, the nose and part of the mouth visible. The rest of the face is worn. The piece has a flat back and rough sides.

This ceramic figurine fragment may originate from the Mesoamerican Zapotec culture of the Valley of Oaxaca, who created ‘ancestor figures’ or offering vessels, often found in burial tombs. Complete Zapotec figurines depict similar characteristics as seen here, such as the headdress and spool earrings. Press molding techniques for creating ceramic figurines were used by some cultures, such as Teotihuacan, that were influenced by Zapotec culture.

A Kundika or funerary vessel with a white glaze and almost globular body. It has a tall slender neck surmounted by a flange top with a tapering nozzle which is decorated with a series of horizontal bands.

Possibily a gilded brass ceremonial charm that was used to decorate ceremonial dress in the Kingdom of Benin (object is currently under research). It is conical in shape with a loop at the narrow end and a mouth at the wide end. The body is decorated with incised interlaced decoration.

A yellow glazed pineapple jar. The body and neck are scaled and resemble a pineapple. There are two twisted, scrolled handles. The jar is resting on a foot which has been repaired with plaster, the rim has also been repaired. Tuscan, possibly Pistoia.

This is a chasse or reliquary box in bronze from the late 13th Century. It is house-shaped with the lid and body hinged together. There are suspension rings at each end for suspension from the neck. It is decorated with engraved foliate tendrils. German or Austrian.

A chasse, perhaps a jewellery box, in bronze. It is house-shaped, heavily gilded and with the original lock and key. The roof cresting has a keyhole pattern with three finials, one at either end and one in the middle terminating in knobs. The surface is decorated with angels inside roundels and curvilinear decoration. There are four legs with the feet at right angles and folded outwards.
A chess piece shaped like an animal, perhaps a horse.

column2: Chinese Earthenware Scene or figure group
column3: A Chinese earthenware glazed grotto group depicting figures and houses above a fish-filled river and craggy, tree-covered hills. This was probably used for growing orchids.

A bulbous, blue and white, porcelain vase. The bottom section is made up five vase shapes joined together. Each of the smaller vases has its own narrow neck with a fluted rim. In the centre of the piece there is a tall neck, culminating in a spherical shape at the top, also with a fluted rim. The vase is decorated with flowers, leaves and butterflies.

A figure of Christ as the Good Shepherd in ivory. Christ is shown as a child sitting with the legs crossed and the chin resting on a hand and a lamb on the lap. The figure is set above a scene with a reclining figure at the base and three lambs around a fountain. Water is pouring from the mouth of a carved head. Goa.

This ceramic head fragment likely originates from the Chupícuaro culture of Preclassic Mexico. The Chupícuaro culture was influential in ceramic production, devoting much time to the creation and exporting of ceramic figurines. This figure illustrates some of the characteristics of Chupícuaro figurines, such as the ‘coffee bean’ shaped eyes, and typical centre hair parting of a female figure. This fragment likely dates from the 3rd century BCE–the 4th century CE.

A pottery cinerary urn from the Early Bronze Age. It has been reconstructed and many of the pieces are missing. The rim is decorated with a herring-bone pattern both inside and outside. This cinerary urn was found at Newtown, Caherconlish, Co. Limerick.
A staff-head, possibly, in pipe-clay, consisting of a tube tapering towards the top and decorated with a series of bands. It is topped with a cockerel, the symbol of St Peter. Possibly Netherlands.

A white marble kandela with a rounded body, cylindrical neck and small conical foot. Handles are missing from either side and the rim of the neck is damaged. This was a hanging lamp. Early Cycladic 1/ Grotta-Pelos phase (Plastiras group).
This is an iron collecting box. It is cylindrical in shape with iron bands and two locks with keys. It has a hinged lid with a slit in the top and a rectangular-shaped handle.
An Egyptian column fragment with a bird and Anubis designs on one face.

column2: Comb scenes of the life King David and Bathsheba
column3: A double-edged ivory comb with fine teeth at one side and wide teeth at the other side. It is decorated on both sides in low relief with carved scenes depicting the story of King David and Bathsheba. One side shows King David sitting by a fountain and playing a harp with three women, this is surrounded by floral decoration. The other side shows David, Bathsheba and her husband, Uriah the Hittite, and two female attendants.

A mether carved from a single piece of wood, with incised bands and geometric, chevron-like decoration. It has four handles with deep lobes and an internal base. Extensions form supports for balance. The mouth is sub-rectangular. The body tapers gently into a sub-square. The mouth edge at the corners is worn and chipped. Three handled methers are communal Medieval drinking or storage vessels. Larger vessels contained bog butter and buried in bogs. Four handled methers are a feature of the Gaelic revival.
column7: A mether carved from a single piece of wood, with incised bands and geometric, chevron-like decoration. It has four handles with deep lobes and an internal base. Extensions form supports for balance. The mouth is sub-rectangular. The body tapers gently into a sub-square. The mouth edge at the corners is worn and chipped. Three handled methers are communal Medieval drinking or storage vessels. Larger vessels contained bog butter and buried in bogs. Four handled methers are a feature of the Gaelic revival.

column3: A plaque in bone showing the figure of a man carved in relief. The man is naked and standing with his hands behind his back. Coptic.

column2: Coptic Carved Bone in the shape of a face
column3: A face carved on a piece of curved bone. The face is framed by hair and part of a winged head-dress remains. Coptic

A gold ring with a carved coral head. The gold mount is done en quatre couleurs, a technique which allows the gold to change colour to white, red, green and blue. The coral carving is of an African head, wearing an Arab style turban.
column7: The head dates from the 17th century and the gold ring from the 19th century.

column3: A carved, stone corbel fragment, decorated with an animal head.

A crucifix figure in wood with long hair falling over the right shoulder, the head is falling to the right and the eyes are closed. The figure has socketed arms most of which are missing. The loin-cloth is short, folded horizontally and fastened to the right. The feet are nailed together and there is a spear wound on the left side. There is a modern loop in the back.

A bronze corpus or crucifix figure. The figure is crowned with the hair in ringlets and the head leaning slightly to the right. The feet are side by side and resting on a suppedaneum. The loin-cloth is long and elaborate, it falls below the knees and is fastened to his left, from which folds radiate out. The figure is clothed in a loin-cloth with a decorated belt around the waist. The surface of the loin-cloth is decorated with incised horizontal lines and circles. The figure was originally gilded.

This is a European corpus or crucifix figure made from either pewter or tin. The word Corpus means ‘body’ in latin. The eyes are closed and the feet are nailed together. The nimbus and loin-cloth are gilded. The loin-cloth is short, folded in horizontal folds, and knotted to the figures left in a looped, pleated fold. It is believed to date to the 16th century. The red velvet-covered cross dates from a later period.

An anhydrite jar with a narrow neck and a broad everted rim which is chipped. The body of the jar is decorated in relief with a row of monkeys with long tails. Ancient Egypt, Middle Kingdom, Second Intermediate Period.

A small earthenware pot, its upper section partially covered in mottled green glaze. The pot has a deep small foot and wide irregular spherical body. The neck narrows and the lip is wide. This is possibly Tudor Green Ware with a label noting Vandon Street, London. It is unclear if this refers to a findspot. The pot is English made but is a copy of typical French ware. The small jar may have contained cosmetics or ointments.
A green crackleware jar with a curved lip. Chinese or Korean.

A lead crucifix known as a penal cross. The front shows a simplified figure of Christ with the feet nailed together and with a nimbus around his head. The back is incised with a heart, cross and the letters IHS and a date. This type of cross is believed to be a souvenir from the pilgrimage site at Lough Derg, Co. Donegal. Lead is an unusual metal to use in the making of penal crosses.

A Crucifix in rosewood with boxwood corpus. There are ornate gilt metal terminals on the cross arms and upper shaft. The base is hexagonal. The crucifix figure has a short flowing loin-cloth, a crown of thorns and the feet nailed together. There is a INRI plaque over the head and there was an ivory skull attached below the feet, this is now missing. This piece was probably made by Andrea Fantoini of Bergamo, Italy.
A cubical ivory bead which is rounded off at the back. It is one of a set of three. There is a design carved on one of the faces and a hole pierced through two of the sides.
A cubical ivory bead which is rounded off at the back. It is one of a set of three. There is a design carved on one of the faces and a hole pierced through two of the sides.
A cubical ivory bead which is rounded off at the back. It is one of a set of three. There is a design carved on one of the faces and a hole pierced through two of the sides.
A blue and white porcelain trumpet-shaped vase which has been cut-down. The vase is decorated with flowers and stylized leaves. Kang-Hsi.

A spherical handwarmer (chafing ball) in cast bronze. Cast in two sections which screw together, it is decorated with a foliate design of stems, leaves and flowers. Inside there is a self-balancing receptacle for hot charcoal.

An Irish delftware plate with a scalloped edge. The rim is decorated with swags and in the centre is a landscape scene with a church. This is one of a pair with HCL 032. These plates were made in Dublin at the Worlds End Pottery of Delamain & Co., c. 1755-1780.

This steel die is octagonal in shape and made by William Mossop (1751-1805), Dublin. The die shows the draped bust of William Deane with the inscription GULIELMUS DEANE ARM and MOSSOP. One of the octagonal sides is inscribed with the number 3 and R WOOD.
A dodecahedron, perhaps a ritual or game item in bronze, with twelve sides, pierced with twelve holes of varying diameters, and with a boss / knob at each corner of the junctions of the facets.
A drinking-horn with metal gilt mounts. The horn rests on claw feet. The rim of the horn is incised with lettering.
A stoneware drinking-jug or tankard, known as tigerware due to its mottled surface. It has a round foot, globular body, long neck and a single handle. It is without mounts. German, Rhenish, Raeren.
A droop-cup with a small round foot, a round bowl and large, angular handles. It is black and decorated with red figures of a man and a woman with floral decoration in between.

A droop-cup with a small round foot, a round bowl and large, angular handles. It is black and decorated on the interior with the figure of a man in red and on the exterior with human and animal heads and stylized flowers.
A droop-cup with a small round foot, a round bowl and large, angular handles. It is black and decorated on the interior with a floral motif. Greek, Attic.

A drug-jar cylindrical in shape and decorated on the front. It has a rectangular, yellow frame intertwined with stylized leaves surrounding the words: Ung. de Thutia. In the centre top of the frame there is an oval surrounding a tree and a serpent. Over the oval there is scrolled decoration. This is one of pair (A-B). This may have contained a crude ointment of zinc oxide.

column2: Drug-jar (albarello) with portrait of a man
column3: An Italian albarello or drug-jar, of waisted cylindrical shape. On the centre-front is a portrait of a man in an oval frame which is surrounded by foliated, scroll work and sgraffito in blue, yellow and white. Similar to CG 036 A. These popular portrait pieces emphasize character rather than beauty. Sicilian, possibly Caltagirone.

A Dublin delftware bowl painted with the three-window house pattern. The inside of the bowl bears an inscription More Rum and Sugar. A painters number 2 is painted on the base of the bowl. The pattern matches excavated examples from Williamsburg, Virginia, USA. [Pictured in the book Irish Delftware by Peter Francis.]
This is a glazed oil-lamp with a strap handle. The rim is curved inwards to form a lip.
A glazed pot with two handles and a twisted strap which is not part of the original piece.
An earthenware pot with an narrow foot, off-white with a speckled blue glaze.

This travertine (Egyptian alabaster) jar is carved using the veins in the stone to create bands around the body of the vessel. It has a flared rim, stepped base and may have been lidded. Travertine is found in small deposits across the Nile valley and in the Early Period was used in pavements and wall linings of temple passages. Travertine was also used in a wide range of canopic jars, statues, bowls and dishes.

A delftware bowl with a metal rim, possibly brass, there is floral decoration internally and externally. The floral decoration in the interior of the bowl is known as the Chinese Windowbox pattern. Probably English.
A bronze Etruscan oinochoe or jug with an upward flanged spout, slightly tapered body and flattened foot. The rim has snake-headed terminals and the handle has foliate decoration at the base.

A travelling toilet set with a folding scissors and compartments to hold other toilet articles inside. The case is decorated with a fish design in amber and glass within a gold frame. A fishtail pattern is created with wire underneath the glass. Etui is a small case of needles, toothpicks, etc.

A maquette for an evening gown in cream, designed by Sybil Connolly. This is a miniature version of a dress known as the First Love dress. This design was first shown at a New York fashion show in March 1953 (see Time magazine, March 23 (1953), page 42).

A flask of a pilgrim, white-glazed, with four carrying handles and narrow neck. It is decorated in green, blue and yellow with a picture of an archbishop or saint with a crozier and a halo behind his head. He is in the act of blessing. He stands in a landscape with two volcanic hills behind him. The scene is surrounded by a scrolled frame. The remainder of the flask is decorated with flowers, leaves and linear decoration.
A polychromed porcelain snipe on a circular base representing foliage. German, Berlin.
A figure of a woman in coral. She is dressed in long robes with a veil on her head. Her hands are joined together in front. The figure represents a saint or the Virgin Mary. Possibly Spanish.

column2: Figure of an animal (possibly a horse)
column3: A leaded bronze statue of a rearing horse, previously belived to be a leopard or panther. The figure is badly damaged with areas missing. The statue is now mounted on a porphyry base. The lower half of the tail and lower portion of the front legs are missing. The front of the muzzle is damaged. The figure appears to be in a low-level rearing position, but the straightened front forearms suggest it was standing on something. The hooves are clearly outlined on the rear legs. The item has been identified as Persian. The Persians were renowned horse breeders and considered the horses value in its functionality. The gift of a horse was seen as a gesture of both favour and practicality.

column2: Figure Of Christ As The Good Shepherd
column3: A figure of Christ as the Good Shepherd in ivory. Christ is shown as a child sitting with the legs crossed and the chin resting on a hand and a lamb on the lap. The figure is set above a scene with a reclining figure at the base and three lambs around a fountain. Water is pouring from the mouth of a carved head. Goa.

This is a German 16th or 17th century painted limewood figure of Christ issuing from a chalice. He is depicted as the Man of Sorrows. He wears a crown of thorns and has his arms crossed at the wrist. Wounds are visible on the hands and side. Only the upper part of the body is visible, the rest is covered by the chalice. The chalice has a round foot, the foot and base of the bowl is decorated with embossed curvilinear motifs.
Description: A figure of a horse in bronze. The body and neck are elongated and there is a loop on the back of the horse.
A figure of St Peter in ivory, dressed in long robes and carrying a key. The figure is set on a drum-shaped base.

An ivory figure of the Virgin Mary. She stands with her hands clasped. Her veil is long deeply folded and draped over her arm. The figure is standing on a square base. This may be from a crucifixion group. Possibly English.
Possibly a figure pendant in ceramic. It is very worn with two perforations.

This seated Madonna and Child is possibly French or Spanish in origin. It is often referred to as ‘Seded Sapentia’ which means ‘Throne of Wisdom’. The Madonna is dressed in a long gown with loose hanging cuffs and is veiled. The infant Jesus is sitting on the edge of the lap of his mother and is dressed in long robes and wearing a crown on his head. The back legs of the chair are modern replacements.

This figure of the Virgin Mary is made from limewood. It is believed to be Spanish and possibly 16th century. The figure of the child which should be on the Virgin’s knee, was lost at point in the past. These types of figures are called ‘Sedes Sapentiae’ meaning ‘Throne of Wisdom’.

column2: Figure sculpture (St Barbara or St Catherine)
column3: A figure sculpture of St Barbara or St Catherine in wood, with original polychrome. It is a half figure.

A ceramic figurine portion orange/brown in colour. The portion shows a head and upper body of a woman, wearing a head-dress, her arm is bent and her hand rests on her breast. It is likely that this figurine is of the the Aztec goddess Cihuacoatl. This figurine would have been hollow and would have contained small ceramic balls so that when shaken would act as a type of rattle, used in fertlity or birth rituals.

A ceramic figurine portion showing the head, shoulders and part of the body. The figure has large ears and is wearing a hat. One of his arms and the collar of his tunic is visible. There are perforations under both armpits and the back is flat. Possibly from Mexico.
A ceramic figurine in yellow. It is of the upper body of a woman with prominent eyes and the breasts visible.
description
A tall splash-glazed flagon jug with a strap handle. This jug has been broken and repaired.

An Early Bronze Age casting mould for flat copper or bronze tools. One face contains a matrix for a flat axe and a smaller axe or chisel-like implement; the opposing one has a matrix for a lightly larger flat axe. The edges of the mould have been shaped by pecking, the face with the matrix remains irregular suggesting it is unlikely a cover would have been fitted on top. As the Bronze Age progressed, more complex two-piece moulds were developed.
A flint dagger with a slightly splayed tang. The edges of the blade are rough and chipped on one side
A flint dagger with a long handle and pressure flaking on the blade. The handle is diamond-shaped in section to facilitate gripping.

A chalice in silver known as the Galway Chalice. This is a travelling chalice which can be dismantled into three parts: the bowl, the stem and the foot. The bowl and stem can fit into the foot which has an angular base and is incised with Christ on the cross. It has an octagonal-shaped foot engraved with a crucifix on a mount. The chalice has the mark of a Galway silversmith (E.G.) and the letters FTD are engraved at the foot of the cross. This chalice closely resembles the Elizabeth Forth Chalice, made for the Friars Minor of Galway, dated 1633.
A game-piece in ivory. It is drum-shaped and perforated through its length and at the side. It is decorated with incised lines and circles
A draughtsman or game-piece in bone. It is sub-circular with incised decoration.
A circular draughtsman or game-piece. It is decorated with a dancing scene on one side and people playing musical instruments, perhaps bagpipes, on the other.
A circular draughtsman or game-piece. It is decorated with a dancing scene on one side and people playing musical instruments, perhaps bagpipes, on the other.

A bourdaloue or ladies travelling chamberpot. The interior, rim, base and handle are all in gilt. The body of the pot is green with gilt decoration in the French Empire style using Egyptian motifs. It took its more general name from a Jesuit father, one Louis Bourdaloue, whose long sermons, preached at Versailles, were extremely popular, especially with the ladies of the court who, in order to secure a seat, used to arrive hours before the scheduled time of the sermon.
A gold penannular ring with overlapping terminals.
A gold pomander in the form of a snail shell. It is hinged on one side with a simple locking pin on the other. The letter E is inscribed on the inner lid. Possibly Swiss.
A gold ring with a grotesque satyr mask.
A gold ring with a coat of arms intaglio.

This piece is a votive figure from the ancient Muisca Civilization in what is now Colombia. These votive figures, called Tunjo, were part of important ceremonies worshiping the goddess Guatavita. Due to the abundance and importance of gold in the Muisca Civilization, these worship ceremonies involved throwing golden tunjos, gold power, and other gold artefacts into Guatavita’s lake.

This piece is a votive figure from the ancient Muisca Civilization in what is now Colombia. These votive figures, called Tunjo, were part of important ceremonies worshiping the goddess Guatavita. Due to the abundance and importance of gold in the Muisca Civilization, these worship ceremonies involved throwing golden tunjos, gold power, and other gold artefacts into Guatavita’s lake.

This fourth or fifth-century vase originates in a group known as ‘plastic vases’, including human figures, body parts, animals and birds. A hand clasps a lekythos, the mouth, neck and part of the body are visible. The whiteness and daintiness of the worn hand indicate a woman. The thumb is over the first two fingers and there is a gap between the small and third fingers. The hand vase rests on an oval base. This personal object was for use by a woman or in a her grave. It possibly contained perfumed oil. Many like this come from eastern Greece, particularly Rhodes, but also Corinth, Athens and the south Italian Greek colonies.

A small earthenware pot, its upper section, partially covered in mottled green glaze. The pot has a deep small foot and wide irregular spherical body. The neck narrows and the lip is wide and slightly everted. This is possible Tudor Green Ware with a label noting Vandon Street, London. It is unclear if this refers to a findspot. The pot is English made but is a copy of typical French ware. The small jar may have contained cosmetics or ointments.

This jug is small, squat with a spherical body and partially glazed with a mottled yellowish-green glaze. The wheel-thrown body sits on a flat base and a tall neck rises to a flattened, slightly everted rim containing a small spout. The fabric is buff with the upper two thirds glazed. A strap handle is attached on one side from the shoulder to the rim. The body is ridged with larger applied decoration encircling the body just below the handle and just above the handle where it is attached to the shoulder. This decoration comprises two simple bands. The glaze is unevenly applied and drip dried in sections almost to the base. There are larger areas of glaze missing and chipped.

This reliquary cross is made in two pieces, which, when put together, form a box in the shape of a crucifix, perhaps to contain a relic of the true cross. The front depicts the figure of Christ on the cross under the hand of God. Christ’s foot overhangs the frame and the finely carved loin-cloth falls below the knee. The eyes are inlaid with either jet or paste. The reverse shows the Agnus Dei within a quatrefoil surrounded by the symbols of the Four Evangelists.

column2: Handle or haft for an adze or hoe
column3: A wooden handle or haft for an adze or hoe.
A ceramic head, possibly from a figurine. It is brown in colour and is shown with a pointed head-dress. The face is worn.
A ceramic head, possibly from a figurine, with a collar and wearing a hat. The face is well worn.
A hood for a hawk in leather and red velvet with a plume of feathers on top. It is closed by a cord at the back. It is on a wooden stand.

column2: Hors-d oeuvre or sweetmeat set Laid out
column3: A sweetmeat or supper dish set in Irish delftware. The largest dish is octagonal in shape with a wavy edge, it is the base for a set of five other dishes (HCL 037-HCL 041). The dishes are decorated with blue floral motifs. The five smaller dishes interlock, they consist of a central dish with four around it, each curved in a quarter of an arc. The entire set is a direct copy of a Chinese design.

column2: Hors D Oeuvre Or Sweetmeat Set
column3: A sweetmeat or supper dish set in Irish delftware. The largest dish is octagonal in shape with a wavy edge, it is the base for a set of five other dishes (HCL 037-HCL 041). The dishes are decorated with blue floral motifs. The five smaller dishes interlock, they consist of a central dish with four around it, each curved in a quarter of an arc. The entire set is a direct copy of a Chinese design.

This aquamanile, hollow cast in copper-alloy, takes the form of a horse. A dragon, forms a handle, and holds the short reins. There is a hinged lid on the horse’s head and a tap with a spigot plug in the lower chest. The handle and reins and spigot were made separately and attached by soldering. The Latin term aquamanile is conventionally applied to vessels from which water was poured for hand-washing in both domestic and liturgical contexts. Most aquamanila in copper-alloy were cast using the cere perdue method and European examples date from the twelfth to the fifteenth century. By 1400 Nuremberg was becoming a major centre for artistic production, in particular metal work.

The Hunt Museum - Horse Outside project started in 2011. The second horse was added in 2012. It was a community project with Angela Connolly, a community artist who worked with two groups of children to design and paint two life sized fiberglass horses with objects from the Hunt Museum Collection as well as personal notes and drawings. The horse are displayed outside the front door of the Hunt Museum on a daily basis during opening hours. Horse Outside is also the title of a comedy song performed by Limerick Duo ‘The Rubberbandits’.
This cup was created during the ICTeens project organised by the Hunt Museum.

A bone ice-skate which is flattened on one side. It has a tapered upturned head with two perforations, one on either side.

A ceramic Imari ware covered bowl with silver mounts. The body is cylindrical with two round handles with scrolled ends. The lid is domed with an animal, perhaps a lion, and flower knob on the lid. The bowl is decorated in a palette of underglaze blue and overglaze red and gold. There is a silver mount around the rim marked HS, possibly added when the bowl arrived in Europe.

An Early Bronze Age ‘Food Vessel’ with an angular profile, with zoned incised decoration on the internal rim and body There is a vertical ladder pattern on the rim/neck; a band of alternate vertical and horizontal panels on the shoulder with a herringbone design beneath. The lower body has infilled chevron patterning and a herringbone motif. The vase is an insular Irish tradition often found in cist graves. This vase comes from Mitchelstown, Co. Cork.

This carved wooden inkwell has three legs and a lead-lined well. The top is domed with the well set in the centre, beneath this there is a plain and an incised ridge and three carved faces, each one set in the centre between the carved legs. The piece is carved from the root of a tree.
An Irish delft-dish, it is circular and decorated with blue flowers and pseudo Chinese motifs. Probably Irish.

A roughly hewn polished stone lamp typical of the Scottish and Irish Iron Age. A short handle protrudes from the side and the rim is decorated in a single continuous line of chevron detail. Described by William Knowles as being of a ‘class of cups or goblets which were placed beside most of the public wells in pagan times.’ This object was found in Connor, Co. Antrim.
An ivory casket with gilded metal, roped mounts set with jewels and a large central lockplate, probably a later addition.

A diptych leaf (dexter) in ivory, showing scenes of the labours of life in two registers. The upper shows the expulsion from the Garden of Eden and the lower register the results of the Fall, showing people toiling. One of the figures in the bottom register is damaged.

Ivory carving of a man seated on a narrow bench. The seat is rectangular, round topped with a partial low straight back. Fabric is draped in folds over the front of the bench and hangs straight down the back. The man is seated with one leg (now missing) out to the side and an arm (now missing) stretched to the same side. Both arms are missing from below the shoulder. The man has well defined muscles in his leg and his foot is shod in openwork sandals tied in wrappings which reach up around his shins. He is dressed in a classical style, knee length toga draped over his left shoulder. A narrow belt is secured around his waist. He is bearded and his hair reaches to the nape of his neck and is curled around the fringe and ends.

column2: Ivory figure of St John The Evangelist
column3: A 13th century AD figure of a man in ivory and polychrome with a wooden peg in the base. The figure is of St John. He is shown as a young man, dressed in long robes and holding a book in his hand.

This carving from walrus ivory depicts the scene leading up to the murder of St Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170 by followers King Henry II. One knight holds an axe with which to break down the door of the Cathedral. There are two tonsured figures in the centre; the hole between them may have held a cross. The three figures to the front include an archbishop (or bishop) holding a staff and two clergymen.

n ivory gravoir or hair parter. It is cream-coloured with traces of brown stain. The gravoir is carved to conform to the bend of the tusk from which it is carved. It is carved with a scene of a couple embracing, possibly Tristan and Isolde. He lifts his hand to caress her face. He wears a short tunic and belt with a deep gole over his shoulders and she is dressed in a long gown.

column2: Ivory Head of the Virgin Mary
column3: A head of the Virgin Mary. She is veiled and wearing a crown; part of the neck of her gown is also visible. This head fits CG 016 (headless Madonna and Child), as does MG 016 (head of young Christ). If these are all part of the same piece it may indicate that the piece dates from the 14th century.

A Siculo-Arabic casket in elephant ivory with gilt copper mounts and with a slightly later lockplate. The casket is made up of large plates of ivory with gilt copper fittings terminating in swelling beak-like forms. The top is hinged to the body and the casket rest on four round feet which may be modern. The lockplate dates from the first half of the 13th century (probably fitted in Germany), the feet are modern.

A Madonna and Child in elephant ivory. The figures are without heads. The Madonna is seated on a low, cushioned throne with carved ends. She is holding the child against her upper body and the child reaches towards her chin. Their clothing is deeply folded and follows the contours of their bodies. The head MG 017 (Ivory head of the Virgin Mary) fits, as does MG 016 (head of young Christ). If these are all part of the same piece it may indicate that the piece dates from the 14th century.

Ivory carving of a man seated on a bench. The rectangular seat has a low straight back. Fabric is draped in folds over the front of the bench and hangs straight down the back. The man is seated with one leg out to the side and an arm (now missing) stretched to the same side. The man has well defined leg muscles. His feet are shod in openwork sandals tied in wrappings reaching up around his shins. He is dressed in a classical style, knee length toga draped over his left shoulder. A narrow belt is secured around his waist. He appears to not be wearing a tunic. He is bearded and his hair reaches to the nape of his neck and is curled around the fringe and ends. The carving is in the classical style and dates to the seventeenth or eighteenth century.
A memento mori (1 of 4) in ivory. It is a janiform head with the head of Christ on one side and a skull on the other. It is stained brown. This may have come from a rosary.
A memento mori (1 of 4) in ivory. It is a janiform head with the head of Christ on one side and a skull on the other. It is stained brown. This may have come from a rosary.
A memento mori (1 of 4) in ivory. This is a carving of a skull. This may have come from a rosary.
A memento mori (1 of 4) in ivory. It is a janiform head with the head of Christ on one side and a skull on the other. The piece is stained brown. This may have come from a rosary.
A whalebone or walrus ivory club, which is highly polished.
A portion of a consular panel in ivory, showing part of the standing figure of a man. The edge of the panel is pierced at regular intervals for attachment to something else.

An ivory panel or plaque showing a recumbent Virgin on a bed with the Infant Jesus at her side in swaddling clothes and the ox and the ass looking on with a small animal in the right-hand corner. It is perforated on the left-hand side of the panel in the centre.

Plaque was likely part of a treasure binding, carved with scenes. 12th century AD. Top: the Annunciation (Mary and the Angel Gabriel) and the Visitation (Mary and Elizabeth). The Nativity with Mary lying on a bed and the Infant Christ just above her being warmed by the ox and ass. A figure stands on either side of this scene, possibly Salomé (the midwife) and Joseph. Bottom: Jesus is being presented by Mary to a male figure carrying doves. In the bottom left-hand corner the Massacre of the Innocents is depicted. Mosan or German.
Very little is known about this object. An ivory pot, the long bowl standing with three legs on a circular base. Possibly African.
Oliphant, a curved ivory, side-blown trumpet made from the tusk of an elephant. There is a brass rim fitted to the open end of the trumpet and a round mouth-piece near the narrow closed top.

column2: Japanese Aritaware porcelain figure of a puppy
column3: A porcelain dog, white with black spots and wearing a red collar with a bell [?]. His tail is curled behind him and he looks upward. Similar to MG 117 B but not made in the same period. Puppies are associated with good luck and protection from evil. They are usually given to newborn baby boys to keep them safe from harm. Arita province.
A tea-bowl used in a Japanese tea-ceremony. The bowl is made of a series of coils visible on the outside. The bowl has been broken and repaired.
A stone jar or pyxis. It is spherical in shape with two sting holes and a thin sloped rim. Possibly Egypt.

A jardinière or plant holder made as a bust of a man in earthenware or faience. The man has long wavy hair and there is a hollow at the back of the head where a plant could be inserted. This object is a copy of a classical sculpture from the Uffizi in Florence titled ‘Head of the so-called Dying Alexander’ and dating from the late 2nd century B.C.

A dagger with probably an original blade, which is narrow with gently curving sides. The hilt, which is probably 19th or 20th century, is faceted and decorated with herring-bone, zigzag and dog-tooth ornament. There are five fake rivet heads on each face.
A bronze key with a ring handle
A handle from an knife in bone. It is decorated with incised lines and has a series of holes. Possibly Viking.

File of material relating to a decorated bronze knife. Includes photocopy of object description sheet which includes sketch of object (date unspecified); photocopy of document (3 December 1994) which comprises comments made by Michael Ryan about various objects in the Hunt Museum. In relation to present object, states that George Eogan might be asked to comment on it and questions if it is Mediterranean; Hunt Museum object comment sheet (22 May 1995) which relates comments of Doctor Otto Urban about object. States that this is a Hallstatt B type object and provides name of person in Vienna who might be contacted for opinion on object.
A bronze penannular bracelet decorated with all-over knobbed decoration. It also has knobbed terminals.

A tazza in lapis lazuli with silver-gilt mounts and stem. The rim has a beaded motif, and the centrepiece is a rosette of flowers and leaves. The stem is cast and features a repeated motif of alternating rams and lions heads, with pendant sprays and swags, between rings, and an upright palmette motif on its base. The base has a cut-card rim. Recessed under the base is a plate with four ovoid cut-outs, each framed in a cartouche, four panels of fruit and a central rosette, all chased.

column2: Late Bronze Age Socketed and Looped Axe
column3: This bag-shaped, looped socketed axe weighing 293.4g, has a slightly uneven, rounded mouth, slight bevel on the rim and short collar. A thick loop is set at its base. The cutting edge is well expanded with very little wear. The blade surface is smoothened, the rest pitted and rough. The patina is mottled brown and dull. A half-rib extends half way to the rim. The findspot is Limerick. These axes are predominant in Late Bronze Age Ireland with 1,300+ examples.

Circular, Yetholm type shield of thin sheet-bronze, beaten to an even thickness of 0.5mm. Decorated with 11 concentric repoussé ribs and 11 rows of low hemispherical bosses with a hollow, rounded conical central boss. The rim is rolled over. Six tears and one perforation represent damage from the rear and front. It is unlikely that this object was ever used in combat. Yetholm shields have been found in England (15), Scotland (9), Wales (2) and Ireland (2). This one was recovered from the Thames at Halliford Upper, Walton-on-Thames.
An oak lectern with space for a book on either side of the gabled double slope. The height can be adjusted and it can be rotated.

A vase or lekythos with a round base, a tall body which is wide at the shoulder and narrower at the base, a tall neck and a deep rim splaying outward. The vase has a tall strap handle ending at the shoulder. The body has geometric decoration with leaves on a white background. This vessel would have contained oil and was a grave offering.

column2: Limestone Statue of god Thoth as a Baboon
column3: A baboon carved from limestone, squats with forearms resting on its knees. A hole in the crown indicates a headdress, a gilded wood sun disc or moon. The smooth face and shoulders indicates the Later Period rather than a New Kingdom hamadryas. The baboon was a manifestation of the god Thoth, a moon deity, who personified divine speech and was a god of writing, mathematics, astronomy and healing. Baboons were common at the animal necropolis in North Saqqara.

A 13th century Limoges reliquary chasse in enamelled bronze. The front shows the murder of St Martial who was one of the patron saints of Limoges, and the ends with figures of saints standing between roundels. Both the back of the chasse and of the lid show enamelled roundel decoration, while the front of the lid shows Christ in Majesty in a circle flanked by angels. At a later date (c.15th century), crocketed gables and pierced roof-cresting were added, plus lion feet to support the crocketed sideposts on which it stood.
