A maiolica tazza (plate or dish) with a highly polished glaze. It has a ribbed stem and circular foot. It is decorated internally in the centre with a scene of a woman in profile (Bella Donna) smelling a flower. A sunburst or dog-tooth motif surrounds this scene with stylized sunflowers. The rim is decorated with a series of concentric lines between which there is a fish-scale decoration. The sunburst and floral motifs are repeated on the exterior. Italian, Deruta.

A polychrome figure sculpture of the Madonna and Child in limestone. The Virgin is crowned, with a pendant veil and wearing a long draped gown. Mary carries the Infant Jesus on her hip and is gently holding his foot. The top half of the child is missing. There are traces of original paint on the statue. 14th or 15th century AD, Burgundy.

A figure of Virgin and child in pipe-clay. The Virgin is dressed in long robes and wearing a long veil and crown, the child rests on her left hip. The Mother and Child hold hands and the Infant holds her left wrist. This piece is made from a mould and may have been used as a staff mount. This object is likely Dutch.

A pharmacy jar or albarello in maiolica, it is basically cylindrical in shape and slightly waisted. It is narrowed at the foot and at the neck with an everted rim. It is decorated with floral motifs in blue and is inscribed: COMM 7 or (s), in the centre. It possibly contained dry ground or powdered cumin. The decoration is similar to that found on 15th century Spanish imports. Italian, Faenza or Venice.

A maiolica jar with spout and handle and a decorative twisted-wire effect between the neck and the spout. It has an everted rim and a narrow, round foot. The body is decorated, in blue, yellow, black and white glaze and inscribed: AAs ROSATI, below the spout and the date 1544. The back is white with blue scrolled decoration. It is decorated with troffei (trophies) and possibly contained rosewater. Italian, Castel Durante.

A glazed maiolica jar decorated with the image of an angel with the inscription underneath TRODREVBARO. It has a lid with a central knob surrounded by floral motifs. The back is plain. Small jars such as this generally contained medication in tablet or lozenge form, in this case of rhubarba purgative.

A broad oviform maiolica pharmacy jar. It is painted in strong foliate design with acanthus leaves and flowers, large and small white flowers and berries, in blue, purple, yellow, green, brown and white. There is an escutcheon on the front bearing the letters IHS with a cross and three nails surrounded by straight and wavy lines. Around this there is the inscription Societas Iesu [Society of Jesus]. Below the crest and inscription are the words Oximel Sinp, in a decorative white band. Oximel simplex was a mixture of honey and vinegar. Possibly one of a group of drug-jars made for the Jesuit pharmacy at Novellara, Reggio Emilia, Italy.

A maiolica jar with a pair of applied, ornate handles in the shape of sea-horses and a short spout. The body of the jar bears the arms of the Order of St Francis (Franciscans) surrounded by fruit and floral decoration. The reverse is decorated with stylized pinecones, a form of the Persian palmette. The jar may have contained syrup, oil or medicated waters. Italian.

A drug jar (albarello) in maiolica, it is tubular with a slightly concave body, narrower at the foot and mouth. It is decorated with rows of blue and yellow flowers between lined triangles. The decoration is derived from Valencian leaf decoration. There is a inscription in a band across the body: dia galauga, or, galanga. This may refer to a herbal medication for the treatment of flatulence and sea-sickness.
A figure of a man in ivory, perhaps St John. The figure is dressed in long robes and has short curly hair. One hand is missing. The piece is set on a velvet stand and backdrop.
A figure of a bird in marble. It is headless and set on an oval flat base. The feathers are well-defined.
A green marble seal with incised characters. It is rectangular in shape with a handle cut out of the marble at the back.

A gilded bronze donkey with a bridle of browband, noseband, cheek-strap and throat-strap. A hole in its back suggests a saddle or pannier. The gilding has mostly worn away on the centre back. The four hooves are clearly defined and the long tail hangs straight. The ears sit up straight and the mouth is slightly open. Opposing holes on the mouth suggest a bit and reins were attached. Domestic donkeys have origins in Egypt c.4000BC. They were vital to trade route expansion and later the Roman Empire relied on donkeys as pack animals to navigate routes such as the Silk Road from the second-century BC.
A money-box, globular in shape, wheel-turned and with a slot in upper side. It has an expanded foot with a small stalk on top in the centre.
A grey pottery storage jar decorated at the neck, with a row of impressed discs, below the everted rim.
A sword-pommel in bronze. It is semi-circular and hollow, bearing a lion and unicorn design in very low relief.
A mether/ meadair, a drinking cup, in wood. It is four-sided with three angular handles, elongated at the end, so they end parallel to the base.

A mether/ meadair, a drinking cup, in wood. It is four-sided with three handles remaining and incised decoration on the body. The handles are angular with elongated ends. This was a communal drinking vessel.
A mether/ meadair, a drinking cup, in wood. It has four flat sides, tapering in at the bottom and with two angular handles. This is a communal drink vessel.

A mether/ meadair, a drinking cup, in wood. It has four sides and three flat handles, rounded at the top and lobed at the bottom. The fourth handle is missing. This was used as a communal drinking cup.
A stone mould with a cross impression on one face. Possibly Byzantine or Eastern Mediterranean.
A stone mould for religious medals with an angel, crosses, medallions and an unknown item. Spanish or Italian, 17th Century AD.

A stone mould with two circular impressions, one of a male face and the other with many faces. There are iron nails in the stone on one side of the impressions and sockets for two more on the other side.
A mount for a staff in gilded bronze. It is six-sided, hollow and decorated with a floral motif within a diamond-shaped panel on each side. The sides are enamelled in blue and red.

A mount, possibly for a harpoon, in shell or bone. The piece consists of an oval, carved at each end with a stylized human head wearing a helmet with a nose-guard. The oval is attached to a curved band with a hole pierced through each end.

An incense boat in gilt bronze, it has an oval body with a flat top and a six-sided stem and foot. There are two lids hinged in centre. The lid is decorated with a floral motif and two serpents curving up from the lid. Probably German, 15th century.
Necklace set with “Irish diamonds” with shamrocks and harp motifs.

This adze weighs 219g, has a plano-convex cross section, curved, asymmetrical edges, asymmetrical blade and rounded, almost flat, butt. The blade and faces are ground and the blade is polished and sharp. Pecking is on the face and butt. One face has a groove along the centre of its length. The findspot is Newcastle, Ballymahon, Longford. Dolerite is predominantly found in the north-east.

This axe weighs 296g, has a full oval cross-section, curved symmetrical edges and asymmetrical blade. The blade, sides and faces are ground and polished. The butt is ground. Depressions on one side may indicate hafting. The edge is sharp. The findspot is Rockbarton Bog, Lough Gur, Limerick. There are two Irish sources for porcellanite, Tievebulliagh, Co. Antrim and Brockley, Rathlin Island. Both utilised in Prehistory.

This axe weighs 416g, has a full oval cross-section, curved edge shape, asymmetrical blade and a rounded butt. The blade, sides, butt and faces are ground and the blade, sides and faces are polished. The edge is sharp but chipped. The blade area is defined by a higher polish. The faces are well ground. A few areas of remnant pecking are both faces. the findspot is Knockderk Limerick. Gabbro comes primarily from Co. Tyrone. Many gabbro axees found in Ireland were imports from Cornwall.

This [axe]http://vocab.getty.edu/page/aat/300024664) weighs 196g, has an oval cross-section, curved, asymmetrical edges, an asymmetrical blade and damaged butt. The blade, sides and faces are ground and polished. Remnant peck marks are visible on the highly polished faces. A clean break crosses the centre of the axe. The findspot is Rockbarton Bog, Lough Gur, Limerick. Dolerite is predominantly found in the north-east.

This axehead weighs 150g. It has a narrow pointed oval cross section and curved, symmetrical edges. It’s blade is symmetrical and it has an irregular butt shape. Only the blade is ground and polished. The sides are pointed and almost straight in plan and the blade edge is chipped. The axe is finely flaked all over. Flint is most common in Ireland in the chalk areas of north-east Antrim.

This axe weighs 40g, has an oval cross section, curved, asymmetrical edges, asymmetrical sharp blade and rounded butt. The blade, sides and faces are ground. The blade and faces are polished. Remnant pecking is visible. Jadeite is from the Alpine (Piedmont) area. In the Neolithic, Alpine quarries of Mont Viso produced small axe and adze-heads which were distributed across Western Europe. Displayed with HCA 172 B. An antler haft or handle for an axehead which is faceted and smooth, suggesting that it has been worked to achieve its present shape. This is probably not original.

This axe weighs 177g, has a narrow oval cross-section, convex edge shape and asymmetrical blade. The blade, butt and faces are ground. The sides are partly ground with flake scars. The edges are sharp but both faces are damaged by post manufacture flake scars and grinding striae. The findspot is Rockbarton Bog, Lough Gur, Limerick. Porcellanite is found in Tievebulliagh, Co. Antrim and Brockley, Rathlin Island. Both utilised in Prehistory.

This axe weighs 478g, has an asymmetrical face, gently curved, asymmetrical edges, asymmetrical blade and rounded butt. The blade, sides, faces and butt are ground but not polished. The sides have remnant flake scars. The edge is blunt, smooth and waterworn. Nodular weathering and exfoliation are evident on both faces. The findspot is Newcastle, Ballymahon, Longford. Pelite occurs across Ireland.

This axe weighs 478g, has a symmetrical cross-section, damaged edges, asymmetrical blade and rounded, almost flat butt. The blade, sides, butt and faces are ground and polished. The sides are slightly splayed. The edge is heavily chipped, worn and blunted. The findspot is Rockbarton Bog, Lough Gur, Limerick. Dolerite predominantly comes from the north-east of Ireland.

The O Dea Mitre is on display in the Museum on behalf of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Limerick. The mitre was made to the order of Bishop Conor O Dea of Limerick in 1418 and still belongs to his successor. This mitre made by Thomas O Carryd would have been used for the most solemn occasions.

An oval dish in Palissy-type ware. It is moulded in high relief and shows a woman dressed in long robes and leaning against a tree. She holds flowers in both hands and has flowers in her hair. By her side there are ceramic pots of flowers and gardening tools. Other figures can be seen in the background. The scene is set within a wheat ear border. French: Avon, near Fontainebleau.

A large dish with an owl perched on a tree surrounded by other birds and trees. The disc, painted in copper green, ochre and manganese, is typical of the type of wares produced in Talavera-Puente during the 18th century. Castile, Talavera-Puente del Arzobispo.
A partially glazed jug with strap handle.
A partially glazed earthenware jug with a strap handle. The glaze is on the upper body handle and both inside and outside the neck.

A wooden cross-shaped pendant showing a stylized human figure. There are two perforations at the top, perhaps for suspension. This type of cross is believed to be a souvenir from the pilgrimage site Lough Derg, Co. Donegal.
A folding, steel penknife with an ivory handle in the shape of a hound. The hound is spotted and has a metal collar.

A valve with moulds for penannular ring-brooches on both sides. One negative is for a ribbed ring with slightly expanded, triangular terminals. Pouring channels are located at the terminal ends. Depressions in two corners indicate where other valve was secured. The reverse has a negative for a plain ring with spheroid terminals and a smaller ring with small spheroid terminals. Pouring channels are visible for both. There is an ogham inscription on one edge.

A drug-jar cylindrical in shape and decorated on the front. It has a rectangular, yellow frame intertwined with stylized leaves surrounding the word: Thamarin. In the centre top of the frame there is an oval surrounding a tree and a serpent. Over the oval there is scrolled decoration. This is one of pair (A-B). This jar possibly contained the the sugared preserved fruit of the tamarind.

A drug-jar with a handle and spout, decorated in blue with bands of simple curvilinear decoration. There is an inscription in black in a band across the body below the handle. The letters GM or CGM are written on the handle. It possibly contained an elixir of myrrh. This jar is very similar to MG 115. Italian, possibly Liguria.

A drug-jar with a handle and spout, decorated in blue with bands of simple curvilinear decoration. It has an inscription in black in a band across the body below the handle. The letters ZR are written on the base of the handle. It possibly contained syrup of jujube. It is very similar to MG 114. Italian, Castel Durante.
A bronze axe with two cutting edges and a central socket. The edges are at right angles to each other.
This porcelain pietà was made in the Meissen factory near Dresden. The quality of the modelling in the Pietà suggests that it may be the work of J. J. Kändler, the outstanding Meissen modeller.

column2: Plate With Border Of Irish Harps And Shamrocks
column3: A circular pearlware plate. It is decorated with a harp and shamrock motif impressed on the border around the rim and a painted zebra in the centre. Irish, Belfast.

Sculpture of a male figure with the arms and head mutilated. This figure shows features of Olmec carvings, downturned mouth, prominent flared lip, bent legs, flat nose, almond eyes and cleft head. Portable objects were made of imported jade and local greenstone. Early evidence of Olmec civilisation dates to 1,200 BC. They lived along the Mexican Gulf Coast, in the Veracruz and Tabasco states. The term Olmec is an Aztec word for the region Olman meaning ‘place of rubber’. More.

A gold memento mori pomander in the form of a highly polished skull. It has deeply sunken eye-sockets and protruding cheekbones. The skull can be opened using the clasp at the top, with the back and front joined together by a hinge. A thin sheet of polished gold, engraved with the inscription: Man proposes but God disposes, separates the back and front of the skull. There are four compartments in the back for perfume or fragrant herbs. The maker is unknown, but the engraving and the inscription suggest English origin. The date 1679 is inscribed on the flat base.

column2: Porcelain Ewer or jug in the form of a woman
column3: A porcelain jug in the form of a Chinese woman, the arms forming the handle and spout. The head is separate sitting into an opening in the neck and acting as a stopper. Qing dynasty.
A porcelain cockerel on an ormolu base. The cockerel is white with the mouth open as if crowing. The bronze base is decorated with leaves and flowers.

A porcelain cat in white with black spots and red fabric tied around the neck. The left paw is raised. Similar to MG 117 A but not made in the same period. Cats are believed to summon good luck and prosperity, and these figures are often placed by the entrance of homes and shops. A raised left paw is thought to beckon customers

A figurine of a woman in 18th century dress with flowers in her hair. Her right arm and left hand are missing. Originally another figure was present but it has been broken off about waist level. One of the shoes of this figure still remains. English, Bow Factory, Stratford Langthorne, Essex.
N/A

column2: Porcelain snuff-box with insects and butterflies
column3: A circular snuff-box of porcelain, painted with insects and butterflies with gold mounts. German, Dresden.
A Meissen porcelain tea-bowl without its saucer. On the outside are painted landscapes set within gilt frames. The inside rim is also decorated with a gilt border.

A blue and white Chinese porcelain vase with a long narrow neck. The vase is decorated with floral motifs which are divided into sections by blue lines, running vertically from the top of the neck almost to the base.
A blue and white Chinese porcelain vase with a narrow neck. The vase is decorated with a willow tree design.

column2: Portion of an Annunciation canopy or baldachin
column3: A portion of a baldachin (canopy / reredos) in carved wood with painted panels. The main painted panel shows the Annunciation, with Mary on the left and the Angel Gabriel on the right with a dove between. There are angels on two, small, curved panels overhead. The words Ave Maria Gratia Plena (Hail Mary, full of grace) are carved in openwork lettering below the main panel (seen here). French or German.
A chamber-pot in pottery with brown and green glaze. It has a rounded body, everted rim and a strap handle.

A Greek pottery cup with red-figure decoration and floral motifs. There are two horizontally mounted handles, one of which was repaired and is now detached together with two shards broken from the rim.
A green glaze pottery jar with two projections at the shoulders of the body, these are pierced, possibly for suspension. The jar has a pot-bellied body and narrow foot with a narrower neck and mouth.
A grey pottery jug with a handle and thumb-print decoration around base. The top has been repaired.
A green-glazed pottery jug with a strap handle
A green-glazed pottery jug with a handle and decorated with one incised band.
A pottery jug with a brown/yellow glaze. It has a single handle and a narrow mouth with an in-turned rim. There is a circular hole in the lower body.
A mug or vessel in pottery. It is brown, relatively tall and slightly waisted with a splayed mouth and single handle.
This porcelain Chinese pug dog is one of a pair with MG 113 A. He is sitting with his tail wrapped around his body and is wearing a bell on a red collar around the neck.
This porcelain Chinese pug dog is one of a pair with MG 113 B. He is sitting with his tail wrapped around his body and is wearing a bell on a red collar around the neck.

A pyx of rock crystal with heavily copper-gilt mounts. It is six-sided with a hinged lid and circular base. There are decorated gilt mounts at the bottom and rim and on the lid rim. There is a crucifix set in the centre of the lid. A pyx is a vessel in which consecrated bread is kept. Probably Venetian.

This bowl has many characteristics of Raqqa ware (northern Syria). Its shape is conical with straight sides and rim. The ceramic body is stone paste or fritware. It is largely unglazed on the exterior. The alkaline turquoise glaze has been thickly applied and has dripped unevenly down the outside rim. The glaze is crazed and has become iridescent due to the salt content in the soil in which it was buried. The simple shape and decoration indicate this bowl was produced for daily use.

A figure of a rearing horse in bronze, on a marble base, that was once reputedly one of three 16th century figures from a cast linked to a drawing by Leonardo Da Vinci. However, the Hunt Museum horse underwent material analysis and x-ray which indicated that it was comprised of 84% copper, 7% tin, 6% lead and 1% zinc, as well as traces of iron, nickel and silver. It has thus been dated to the end of the nineteenth century.

column2: Relief Of A Monk or Cleric
column3: A wooden panel with a monk or cleric, perhaps a Saint, carved in high relief. The figure wears long robes and a cloak which covers his head and is draped across his body. A rare survival. Irish, 15th century.

A figure of a man, an apostle or saint, in walrus ivory. The figure is carved in relief. It is bearded and standing. He is wearing classical dress and holding a scroll in the right hand. This figure is pierced with two holes for attachment. It was attached to the same object as MG 028 A but was carved by a different hand. German, Cologne, 12th century AD.

column2: Relief of man (St John the Baptist)
column3: A figure of St John the Baptist. The figure is carved in relief and was attached to a larger object such as a shrine. He is shown standing, his right shoulder is bare and he is wearing a fur-fringed mantle. He holds a scroll in his left hand. The right hand is a replacement, the right foot is missing and the back is flat. There are two holes in the body for attachment. MG 028 B was attached to the same object but is by a different hand. German, Cologne. German, Cologne, 12th century AD.
This wooden reliquary bust of a cleric has a tonsured head. The bust is polychrome with a rock crystal set in the head beneath which a relic would have been visible.
N/A

A bag-shaped beaker with rounded profile, slightly incurved conical base, narrow foot and cornice rim. A fine white ware with black coating decorated with a trailed slip (barbotine technique) of raised motifs, a hound chasing a hare, dots and frieze of leaves. This is Cologne ware dating to the second or third-century AD with a distribution in the Rhineland and Britain.

This jugs oval body merges into a short flaring neck with an everted rim. It has a delicate narrow base and curving handle with central rib. The body and neck are cast as a single piece. The handle terminates in a volute, beneath is a triangle with the bust of a man, with a beard and tunic fastened by a brooch. Two spirals on either side of his head curve and end below in two spirals above a palmette. The top of the handle ends in a thumb size scallop shell support, on either side of which are two stylized bird’s heads with long beaks emerging from volutes. Underneath this are several concentric circles. This type of jug was made in southern Italy from the mid-first to the third-century AD.

This cast statue has a modern marble base, small head and unpronounced features. Hair is visible at the back of his head but the front is bald. His right hand is raised, his left forms a fist. He is wearing a toga, tunic and boots. His toga is draped over his left shoulder and falls down the left side of his back. It crosses over the front and underneath his right arm. Firing defects cover the body. The face is crudely executed and his left eye has not been cast. A repair is visible above the knees. The stance of the man indicates he was of senatorial rank.

This sheet-bronze strainer has a hemispherical pierced basin, steep sides and an everted rim. Pierced decoration is arranged in double sets of concentric rings framing an interlocking-meander pattern. The base contains a 4 petal rosette motif. The lunate handle opening derives from two swanlike birds placed back to back. Stylistic comparisons can be made with 1st century AD examples from Pompeii and Herculaneum. This strainer demonstrates the accomplished art of metal-workers. It filtered unrefined wine removing sediments and herbs, used as sweeteners.

This Romansque statue, of the Enthroned Madonna, shows Mary as Theotokos (Mother of God), or Sedes Sapientia (the Seat of Wisdom). Such works usually show the Christ child on Mary’s knee, his absence is highlighted by the fixing dowels in Mary’s lap which would have secured him there. This limewood carved statue is German (Lower Rhine) and early 12th century.

A salt-cellar in brass. It is in three parts diminishing in size to the top. The two bottom sections are bell-shaped and the top domed, ending in a pine cone. It is decorated in strap work and scroll decoration. The salt cellar rest on three ball feet. The interior is silver-gilt.

A single-handled jug with silver mounts on the lid, collar, handle and foot. Decorated with a leaf and strapwork neck frieze with cherubs heads in a circle at each end. In the middle there is a heart and mask. The upper slopes of the body are decorated with a criss-cross geometric design and the lower part of the body is decorated with gadrooning. The later mounts are decorated with a floral motif. The thumb plate has a mark, R.B.E. Siegburg stoneware is handmade with a distinctive grey-white glaze. Decoration is pressed on meaning large volumes can be made quickly. These jugs spread afar through the development of trading posts by the Hanseatic League.

A beak-spouted flagon of beaten bronze on a splayed base with a bulbous shoulder, narrow neck and flat rimmed pouring mouth. The cast handle has a terminal on the body, decorated with a palmette, S-spirals and scrolls ending in a lotus flower above and a lyre below. Above, the handle forks ending in two animal heads with setback ears appearing to represent crouching felines. This is a type known as ‘Schnabelkanne’, a distinctly ‘Celtic’ style manufactured from the late sixth-century BC in Etruria. They were often placed in Celtic princely graves and traces of wine have been found in some flagons.

column2: Sculpture of Virgin Mary, St John, Mary Magdalen
column3: An oak figure sculpture of the Virgin Mary who has collapsed and is being supported on either side by St John and Mary Magdalene. This carving may be from the foot of a crucifix. Netherlands, 15th century AD.

A medieval seal matrix in bronze gilt, pointed oval in shape. The front has the image of a standing bishop with three fleur-de-lis on each side and a crown beneath. There is an inscription around the edge which reads: S LUDOVICUS REX FRANCIE ORO MINORUM. The back is shaped in the form of a raised leaf within a raised circle of leaves.
A pointed oval seal matrix with an inscription around the edge. There is a central figure with hands clasped together and standing on a platform over another figure.

An oval seal matrix showing the figure of a bishop or saint with his hand up in blessing and carrying a crozier. There is a figure on either side and over his head. There is an inscription around the edge.

column2: Serving Dish With Butterflies and Bees
column3: A large oval, Meissen porcelain dish with a wavy rim. It is marked with the crossed swords mark underneath. The surface is decorated in the centre and rim with butterflies, moths and other insects. This large serving dish comes from a service of more than 100 pieces commissioned by General Sir Richard Bourke, KCB, of Thornfields, Lisnagry, from the Meissen factory in 1820. The rim also bears a seated heraldic cat with an inscription: A CRUCE SALUS below. This decoration is hand painted and was added at a later date to the manufacture of the plate.

This large carving (0.48m x 0.33m) is the remainder of a larger Sheela-na-gig which was discovered in Caherelly East (LI023-040001) during repair works to a bridge. The stone was placed in one of the support structures of the bridge and workmen alerted John Hunt who was living locally at the time. It was subsequently displayed in the Hunt Museum Collection in Limerick City. The carving is missing its head, left hand and feet, but what remains of the body is skilfully carved. A long body with even breasts and a inset belly button are placed above a large/deep open vulva, and anus. The hands are behind the legs, the right one remains, and has four fingers carved. It is a shame so much of the carving is missing. A spherical depression is located on the back of the stone; it is unknown if this was a carved feature or a natural erosion of the limestone. LI005-017180.
A snuff-box made from a shell with silver mounts.
A shell snuff-box with silver mounts
A snuff-box made from a shell with silver mounts.
A snuff-box made from a shell with silver mounts.
N/A

column2: Si Satchanalai ware jar with lid
column3: A pear-shaped jar with a lid. The lid is stepped with an knob handle. The jar is decorated with blue lines which encircle the base, centre and neck of the jar. Between the lines the body is decorated with a curvilinear leaf pattern. Possibly Thailand.
A 6th-century belt-buckle with interlaced animal decoration set with garnets. Possibly Anglo-Saxon.

A Ming dynasty, Wan Li (1573-1619) (Emperior Xian), porcelain bowl with Elizabethan silver mounts. The outside rim of the bowl is decorated with a flying horse border and the walls are decorated with flower sprays.

From Freugh, Stranraer, Scotland a small ovoid stone decorated with an oval frame, inscribed cross and a central, deep cut circular depression. Pebbles with various cross forms are found across Ireland and in smaller numbers in Scotland. Names given in modern times include altar, prayer, cursing ,priest’s, pilgrim’s and turning stones. The cross gives a religious feel but portable pestles, grinding stones and hammerstones date from the introduction of stone ground technology in the Neolithic.
A snuff-box of shell with silver mounts.
This is a snuff-box, decorated on each face with painted shipping scenes. The box has metal mounts which are possibly silver.
A lozenge-shaped flint spearhead in two pieces. The centre of each face is smooth but the edges are steeply pressure flaked. The butt/tang is slightly rounded as is the point.
A hollow-based flint spearhead with each edge deeply indented.
A flint barbed and tanged spearhead.
A bronze brooch of the spectacle type. It consists of two circular-shaped coils attached to a curved band with a pin and clasp at the back.

A spirit barrel in Irish delftware. It is white with a bung hole in the centre of the long axis and at the edge of one end. It is decorated in blue with two bands of scroll decoration and many plain bands. The barrel is inscribed beside the hole in the long axis with the letters I and F and underneath with the date 1748.

column2: St Anne with the Christ Child & the Virgin Mary
column3: A limewood group of St Anne dressed in a full-length heavily draped robe with traces of gilding and a wimple, holding the naked Christ Child in her arms. By her side the young Virgin with hair hanging to her waist reaches up to touch the child. South German.

column2: St Christopher and the child Jesus
column3: A statue of St Christopher and the child Jesus in painted terracotta. St Christopher is bearded and leaning on a staff and is standing on stones. He is wearing a tunic and a deeply folded cloak. He carries the child, whose head is missing, on his shoulders.

A rearing figure of a stag in silver-gilt. It is believed to be German or Austrian from the 16th century. The hind legs rest on an oval plinth decorated with flowers and leaf motifs. The front quarters are supported by a stem decorated with leaves. This item is hollow and the head can be removed; it was possibly used to hold wine or spirits. German or Austrian.
A stand or base of a vessel in ivory. It is ring-shaped and bearing relief scenes. The carved scenes show the Labours of Hercules. French or German.

Portrait like sculpture of a lower half of a basalt head. The top, back and ears are missing. The left eye survives as the lower frame. The features are soft and rounded with a large round tipped nose and closed lips. Below the location of the left ear is a protruding sub-square lobe which may be the remains of hair or headdress. The base of the head is broken so it’s difficult to assess whether this may once have been part of a larger figurative statue. Egypt, 11th or 12th dynasty or a modern piece that took inspiration from statues of Amenhotep III from the Middle Kingdom (http://n2t.net/ark:/99152/p03wskdgq4n).

A figure of man in wood (acacia negevensis). The figure is nude, in a hieratic stance with the face, arms and feet missing. The figure rests on a modern stand. In the details of its carving, especially of the ear and the groove round the head, and the fact that it is bearded, the statue is closer to Greek work of the later sixth century BC than Egypt figures. This piece may have been an early Egypt carving which was reworked centuries later by a Greek carver. The piece has been carbon dated to c. 2250 BC, Egypt 12th dynasty.
A statue of a male figure in white marble, the torso only remains.
A figure sculpture of Balthasar (one of the Magi) in limewood. Most of the original polychrome (red, gold, green and black) survives. South German.

A figure sculpture of Balthasar (one of the Magi, apparently buried in Cologne). There are still traces of the original polychrome remaining. The figure is carved as wearing a turban, a belted tunic and breeches. Possibly German.
A porcelain figure of woman in 18th century dress with an elaborate hair style and holding a large fan. Possibly Italian.

A carved stone fluted moulding on which sits a portion of a winged rabbit. The terminal of the piece has a carved anthropomorphic stylized face. The rabbit sits on top of the fragment with its mouth open and its ears stretched back. Folded, dragon like wings sit along both sides of its back. Small feet poke out from underneath while its muscled hindlegs give a crouched, ready to spring appearance. The piece is recorded as a tomb-drop. It is possibly a terminal for tracery work of a tomb-canopy, or it may be from similar tracery on the tomb itself. Chest or altar tombs became common in the Medieval period and occupied prominent positions in Church and graveyards.

column2: Stone carving of the head of a man
column3: A carved head of a man in stone, the face is flattened and the figure is bearded. It is perforated at one side near the top.

Partially complete mould for casting small items of jewellery. It is a rectangular stone with one broken end. One face has 2 valves for buttons or pin heads of spiral design. Each is deeply cut to a rounded point with 3 concentric steps. The outline of a third valve is visible. The central valve has an etched outline of a large ring. Two valves have the beginnings of incised pouring channels. Such casting moulds date in Ireland from Prehistory to Medieval times and are found in ringforts and crannógs.

A stoneware jug with silver mounts on the handle, rim and a silver lid. This ware is known as tigerware due to the mottled surface. The mounts are decorated with scrolled floral decoration. The lid is decorated with a large flower, the petals arranged around a central knop. The letters WE are engraved on the knop. Between the lid and the hinge there is a fish or dolphin. The jug is German, Cologne, and the mounts are possibly English.

A serpent or swan head in bronze. There is a double band around the around the neck, perhaps a collar, and incised feathers or scales. The head has been broken off from a larger piece.

The Antrim Cross is a bronze cross with five equal arms from the early 9th century. The cross has five pyramidal bosses each in the form of a truncated pyramid. The side of the pyramids are decorated with interlocking angular fields of yellow enamel, alternating with a similar-coloured design of an arrow within a truncated triangle. The taller central boss and has an animal design. The flat tops are decorated with small squares of millefiori enamel. Rivet-holes in the separately cast base-plate show that this cross was attached another surface. It is the only virtually intact example of its kind and period.

A bronze sanctuary bell from the ninth century known as the Bell of Badoney. Both front and back are widely splayed while the other sides are narrower. It has a small handle on top and the clapper is missing. The bell was found in a bog at Lower Badoney, Co. Tyrone, in 1856. This site forms part of the Journey Through Time, archaeological and historical tour of the Foyle and Sperrins area.

A pyx in silver-gilt. It is cylindrical in shape with a flat, hinged lid. It is secured by a pin attached to a chain and there is a suspension loop on top. The lid is decorated with the figure of Christ on the cross and two inscriptions.

An early Bronze Age food vessel. The tripartite bowl is largely intact, with a bevelled rim with impressed comb decoration; its external surface is divided into three zones by two cordons or raised bands, decorated with triangular motifs. Either incised or comb-stamped lines decorate each zone. There are incised horizontal grooves immediately under the rim, with a band of vertical grooves below this. There is an area of vertical grooving in the middle of the vessel and horizontal comb-impressed lines on the lower section. There are lime accretions on the vessel surface. The bowl was found in Mitchelstown, Co. Cork.

A tripodal candlestick with claw feet, a circular base and cylindrical nozzle with a rim. The candlestick is decorated with a variety of hatched decoration with circles, lozenge shapes and a beaded rim. The nozzle is decorated with dotted bands and interlaced patterns.
A figure, possibly of a monkey, in turquoise. Olmec.

A vase or lekythos with a round base, a tall body which is wide at the shoulder and narrower at the base, a tall neck and a deep rim splaying outward. The vase has a tall strap handle ending at the shoulder. The body has geometric decoration, with leaves and grapes on a white background. This vessel would have contained oil and was a grave offering. H 22; Diam. (at base) 5.75

This is a walrus ivory plaque or carved panel of the crucifixion. The panel is oblong in shape with raised borders. The borders are pierced with eight holes, indicating that the panel was attached to a larger object. The panel shows the figure of Christ resting upon a suppedaneum beneath the hand of God. The cross has raised borders with the symbols of the four Evangelists shown at the corners of the plaque. English, Anglo-Saxon.
A pottery watering-pot with reddish-brown glaze, a flat base and bulbous sprayer rose. It has a single handle, with a raised rim partly covering the mouth. English, Tudor period.

A whalebone panel showing the Ascension. 12th century AD. The figure of Christ is shown rising into the sky with a dove on the right-hand side. Two angels are shown directly underneath Christ. On the bottom of the panel a group of disciples are shown with all of them looking upwards. One figure is standing pointing towards the figure of Christ. A hole is punched through each corner of the panel indicating that it was once attached to something else.
A whistle, probably made of bone, which is hollowed at one end. It has three perforations, two on one side and one on the other.
A Roman drinking-cup with a narrow base. It is colour-coated but heavily abraded.

A large Dublin delftware spirit barrel with a hole in the centre of the long axis and in one of the ends. It is white with manganese decoration of an Italianate landscape and the heraldic crest of the Molyneux family of Castle Dillon, Co. Armagh. Both ends of the barrel are moulded with ribbing.

A wooden and gilt pricket-type candlestick carved on the front with vine scrolls in a spiral twisted shape. There is a metal wax pan on top. This is one of a pair with HCA 30 B. Possibly Flemish, 17th century AD.

A rectangular wooden chest with a convex top and possibly traces of deer skin covering. There are many studs decorating the outside. There is a handle at each end, a lock on one side and lid hinges on the other. The letters E.A.P. spelt out in studs are on top of the lid.

The vase has an angular profile and is decorated entirely with incised grooving. While a herring-bone motif rings the internal rim, the external decoration is zoned. There is a vertical ladder pattern on the rim/ neck, a band of alternate vertical and horizontal panels on the shoulder with a herring-bone design beneath, and the lower body has infilled chevron patterning with a herring-bone motif on the lower section. There is a circular hole in the base. This vessel was found in Mitchelstown, Co. Cork.
